articles.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
articles.excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October."Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch.

articles.title: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extradition
articles.excerpt: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradited to the Republic of Ireland on SundayByGabija GataveckaiteDublin correspondentEimear Flanagan and Barry O'ConnorBBC News NIUpdated 2 hours agoSuspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has appeared before a Dublin court after being extradited from Dubai.He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.An Irish government jet carrying the 49-year-old landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival.Following a 13-minute non-jury hearing at the Special Criminal Court, he was remanded in custody until 5 October.Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April.

articles.title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
articles.excerpt: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years".Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain."This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again."He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."

articles.title: Residents warned to brace for the worst as Canada wildfire rages out of control
articles.excerpt: British Columbia Premier David Eby told a news conference on Saturday that one fire official had likened the fire to "a bomb going off"."Homes have been lost, and properties have been destroyed. Some people became trapped as conditions changed very quickly, and needed to be rescued," the premier said.A state of emergency allows the provincial government access to special powers including travel restrictions and supply protections to prevent price gouging, and extra resources to coordinate rescue work.Summerland, which has a population of about 12,000 people, has been one of the hardest hit areas and forced to evacuate. So were residents in parts of Peachland, which is home to about 6,500 residents."We have been on evacuation alert many times," said Earl Kurz, a Peachland resident of 30 years. "This is the first time we were actually evacuated." Kurz was on a boat with his wife in Okanagan Lake on Friday afternoon, when he saw clear blue skies rapidly turn hazy grey. By nightfall, dark clouds of smoke above a raging wildfire came into view. It was headed towards Kurz. "We watched it from the lake," he said. "It was unreal." Hours later, police knocked on his door and ordered him and his wife to evacuate.Kurz said they are now safe in a camper miles away. The regional districts of Central Okanagan and Okanagan-Similkameen, as well as Snpink'tn Indian Band and the districts of Summerland and Peachland have issued evacuation orders, with evacuation alerts in some areas, according wildfire officials.In Okanagan, there are a lot of horses that residents have been struggling to evacuate, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported. Those unable to relocate their animals left their gates open in the hope the animals would find their own way to safety, local residents told CBC. Some owners also painted markings on their animals to make them easier to identify later, according to the outlet.
articles.summary: 不列颠哥伦比亚省省长戴维·伊比在周六的新闻发布会上表示，一名消防官员将这场大火比作“炸弹爆炸”。“有房屋被烧毁，财产被毁。随着情况迅速变化，一些人被困，需要救援。”省长说。紧急状态赋予省政府特殊权力，包括旅行限制和供应保护以防止价格欺诈，以及协调救援工作的额外资源。人口约1.2万的萨默兰是受灾最严重的地区之一，被迫疏散。皮奇兰部分地区的居民也被迫疏散，当地约有6500名居民。“我们多次接到疏散警报，”在皮奇兰住了30年的居民厄尔·库尔茨说，“这是我们第一次真正被疏散。”库尔茨周五下午与妻子在奥卡纳根湖的船上，看到晴朗蓝天迅速变成灰蒙蒙一片。夜幕降临时，狂暴野火上方的滚滚黑烟映入眼帘，正朝他袭来。“我们在湖上看着它，”他说，“太不真实了。”数小时后，警察敲门命令他和妻子疏散。库尔茨说，他们现已安全抵达数英里外的一辆房车里。据野火官员称，中央奥卡纳根和奥卡纳根-西米卡明地区、斯恩平克廷印第安部落以及萨默兰和皮奇兰地区已发布疏散命令，部分地区发布了疏散警报。加拿大广播公司报道，奥卡纳根地区有许多马匹，居民一直在努力疏散。当地居民告诉CBC，无法转移动物的主人打开大门，希望动物能自行找到安全路径。据该媒体报道，一些主人还在动物身上做标记，以便日后更容易辨认。

articles.title: Ecuador charges ex-minister over presidential candidate assassination case
articles.excerpt: Prosecutors in Ecuador have charged a former interior minister and six others on suspicion of being involved in the assassination of a presidential candidate in 2023.José Serrano and the head of cartel Los Lobos, Wilmer "Pipo" Chavarria, were implicated in the murder of Fernando Villavicencio at a campaign event in the capital, Quito, days before the election.Five people linked to the criminal gang were jailed over the hit in 2024, while Pipo was captured in Spain last year, having faked his own death.Villavicencio, a journalist turned prominent legislator, was known for his anti-corruption stance and was one of few candidates to allege links between organised crime and government officials.He had continued to appear at public campaigns after being given a security detail due to his receiving a number of death threats.Daniel Noboa, who ultimately went on to win the election and become Ecuador's president, has taken a hardline military approach to combatting crime gangs. The five convicted over Villavicencio's murder in 2024 were said to have orchestrated the hit. The alleged gunman was shot dead at the scene, while six other men were found murdered in prison while awaiting trial.The seven named by the Ecuadorean Attorney General's Office on Saturday were accused of playing an indirect role in the killing - many of whom had links to Los Lobos, or "The Wolves", one of the nation's most powerful criminal gangs.Five of these were now considered fugitives, it said.Serrano and Xavier Jordán were currently located in the US, former assemblyman Ronny Aleaga was in Venezuela, while Pipo remained in Spain with an extradition request pending. The Attorney General's Office has requested Interpol red notices for their capture and extradition.Ángel Esteban Aguilar, also known as Lobo Menor, was arrested in Mexico City in March and returned to Ecuador after a red notice was issued over the murder of Villavicencio.

articles.title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
articles.excerpt: Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems.A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police.It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen.

articles.title: Nigerian army says it safely rescued 33 people kidnapped by gunmen
articles.excerpt: Nigeria's army has said it safely rescued 33 people after they were kidnapped by armed men while travelling through the country's north-western Zamfara state.The army said its troops mobilised alongside the police immediately after hearing about the abduction, in the Tsafe area of Zamfara on Saturday afternoon.The military found the kidnappers in the process of moving the hostages to an unknown location, the army said, and the gunmen fled into the nearby bush after coming under fire.Kidnappings by armed groups who hold people for ransom are common in parts of north-western Nigeria and major roads have become targets for attacks.Analysts say ransom payments by desperate families, intermediaries or, in some cases, Nigerian authorities have fuelled the abductions.Nigerian army spokesman Lt-Col Aliyu Danja said it was unclear where the abductors were moving their hostages when troops intercepted them, adding that the army was now attempting to track the kidnappers."The troops engaged the terrorists with effective fire, forcing them to abandon the victims and flee into adjoining bushes," he said, noting that all the hostages had been recovered without any casualties.

articles.title: Perez Hilton faces long recovery after reports he self-harmed during livestream
articles.excerpt: The US blogger Perez Hilton is in a "serious but stable" condition after being admitted to hospital, according to his family.Emergency services were called to his Miami home on Tuesday after members of the public reported concerns while watching a TikTok livestream. The Miami sheriff's office confirmed they attended a scene of a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm" on Tuesday. They did not confirm his name but said the man was alone in the house at the time.A statement released on the 48-year-old's website said he "experienced significant blood loss" and his treatment and recovery would be a "long process".If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.The statement, external said Hilton was being held in hospital under Florida's Baker Act, which focuses on providing services for people experiencing a mental health crisis.The father-of-three, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, is expected to have surgery in the coming days. A TikTok spokesman said its automated moderation systems flagged the livestream to the company's US moderation team for review within minutes.A moderator error caused a delay in the removal, TikTok said, but the company alerted law enforcement to the situation, closed several subsequent streams within 90 seconds, and banned the account.The pseudonym Perez Hilton is a reference to Paris Hilton, who was at the height of her fame when the celebrity gossip blog was launched in 2005. The website would go on to attract eight million hits a day at a time when the internet was still in its relative infancy. It was criticised for vicious commentary of stars including Miley Cyrus and Lady Gaga.In later years, Hilton admitted having regrets about being "mean or cruel". He has also appeared on reality TV shows including Celebrity Rap Superstar and Celebrity Big Brother.

articles.title: Puerto Rico rations water supplies due to intense drought
articles.excerpt: Hundreds of thousands of people are going without running water for two days at a time in Puerto Rico, as authorities in the US territory take drastic measures to combat a severe drought.Many households on the Caribbean island have been split into two groups - with each having their water supply shut off for 48 hours on a rotating basis.Residents in the capital, San Juan, where the taps were turned off on Friday, decried the rationing. Officials have not said when the measure will end.Most of Puerto Rico is facing moderate to severe drought conditions, according to the US Drought Monitor, which has been compounded by long-term issues with the island's infrastructure.Puerto Rico's water authority says about 65% of the water it produces is lost or goes unbilled, much of it through leaks and ageing pipes, according to the BBC's US news partner CBS.The island's Governor Jenniffer González has acknowledged these issues, but says rationing was implemented due to the weather, which has left the crucial Carraízo reservoir depleted.Puerto Rico experienced its driest July on record, with 68% of the island currently facing drought conditions.Seven regions usually served by the reservoir have been affected, with 180,000 properties subject to rationing, the government said.González said the decision was taken "after carefully evaluating the current conditions of the Carraízo reservoir in conjunction with weather forecasts"."This situation is beyond our control," she said in a statement.

articles.title: An unbearable rotting stench is plaguing an LA neighbourhood
articles.excerpt: On any typical day, Alexis Sicairos and his girlfriend have a line of patrons waiting to order a banana buzz latte or a cloud matcha at their Los Angeles coffee stand. But now, the street corner where they sit is largely empty.The reason is clear the second you walk into the neighbourhood: it stinks. On 17 June, a fire destroyed a large cold-storage warehouse in the area, leaving behind some 85 million lb (39 million kg) of rotting food, including beef, pork, poultry and seafood. Nearly two months later, residents of Boyle Heights say the clean-up has taken a lot longer than expected and they've grown frustrated with the pungent odour hovering over the area."It smells really bad, like really bad... to the point that you want to throw up," says Mesha, a 37-year-old security guard stationed outside a marijuana dispensary. She likens the smell to that of a dead body.Lineage, the company that operated the warehouse, said that as of Monday about 80% of the food waste had been removed. But city officials said this week that the company's response had "fallen short" and that they have issued public health and safety violation notices.Many residents blame the city for what they deem an inadequate response to the fire and a lack of transparency and resources. "I understand why residents are frustrated," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told the BBC in a statement. "They deserve transparency, clear communication, and meaningful support. Since day one, I have been in Boyle Heights listening to residents, meeting with families, and making sure their voices guide our response."The mayor, who is up for re-election this year, said she directed city departments to work with local, state, federal, nonprofit and community partners to deliver immediate support and solutions.Bass has also issued executive orders to mobilise resources and speed up the cleaning process.

articles.title: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
articles.excerpt: Image source, ReutersBySebastian Usherglobal affairs correspondent, and Callum TulleyReporting fromin Sebastia, occupied West BankUp in the hills above the Roman columns of the ancient site of Sebastia, in the occupied West Bank, are olive fields that have been cultivated for generations by Palestinian families.One of the landowners, Abu Mudif, says he has received notification that his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres that the Israeli authorities are taking possession of in order, they say, to protect and develop the site for a major new national park.Typically, Palestinian landowners receive little or no payment for such land expropriation. And even when it is offered, most refuse it as they see accepting it as giving recognition and legitimacy to the loss of what they see as their patrimony.It's a vital income for Abu Mudif to lose of course, but it goes deeper than that for him.Image caption, Abu Mudif says his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres being expropriated by Israeli authorities"If I wanted to describe it, the closest description I can give is that it is like having your soul ripped away. I cannot imagine myself without my land."Nahed Sakha owns a local restaurant that is under threat of demolition.He says the Israeli plan seems to be to cut Palestinian residents off from the archaeological site, which dates back thousands of years and has significant remains from the ancient Jewish past, as well as many other eras including the Romans, the Crusaders and the Ottomans."Restoration work has now begun along with excavations," he says.

articles.title: Man arrested after boat capsizes near Statue of Liberty killing woman and infant
articles.excerpt: The operator of a boat that overturned near the Statue of Liberty, killing a woman and a baby, has been arrested and charged with reckless endangerment, New York police said.Officials said a large search and rescue operation was launched after the incident near New York Harbour on Saturday night. Twelve people who were initially rescued from the water are all reported to be in stable condition.New York police divers later found a 27-year-old woman and a five-month-old girl, who were transported to a nearby hospital where they later died. The names of passengers and the specific cause of the incident have not been released by officials. Around 22:25 local time (03:25 BST), police received a 911 call reporting an overturned boat in the waters near Liberty Island, which houses the iconic statue. A nearby tour operator Sea the City saw the capsized boat and helped pull 11 people from the water, the company's founder Adam Schwartz said according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.The rescue involved two Coast Guard boats, four fire department boats, two police boats and a police helicopter, the USCG said. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, officials said.The boat's operator, a 46-year-old Manhattan resident, faces 13 counts of reckless endangerment, officials said. Coast Guard investigators are also determining whether the boat was illegally chartered.An illegal charter is any passenger-for-hire vessel operation that does not have required credentials, safety equipment, and certificate of inspection."We are extremely grateful for the heroic, swift actions of our partner agencies and Good Samaritan vessel who assisted in rescuing survivors from the water," said Capt Doreen McCarthy of the USCG.

articles.title: Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait
articles.excerpt: Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran warned that any deal would not see an immediate reopening of the vital waterway.Both sides suggested on Saturday that discussions were progressing, but a timeline on any deal being finalised remained unclear.

articles.title: Spain imposes border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
articles.excerpt: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.Spanish officials said the documents of 5%-10% of passengers were being checked before they were allowed to disembark planes. Italy has also said its border controls are random. The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules.Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the ​border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy.Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta.Italy has said that Spanish and EU citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents.However, it is not clear how border officials were meant to distinguish between EU and non-EU travellers and El Pais has reported that several Italian airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks.As for Spanish controls, the authorities insists the immigration checks are random. However, a passenger arriving in Madrid on Saturday told national broadcaster RTVE that all passengers on her flight had had to show their passports.

articles.title: Child among three killed in Russian missile attacks near Kyiv
articles.excerpt: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said.Another three people were injured as ballistic missiles hit east of Kyiv, head of the regional military administration Timur The new attack comes just days after 21 people were killed as Russia intensifies its strikes, aware that Ukraine has been running out of Western-donated interceptor missiles used to defend its skies.On Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued a fresh call for more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, saying what his country was receiving was not enough.Zelensky's plea comes days after US President Donald Trump appeared to go back on a promise to grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture the defensive systems. On Saturday, Ukraine's president still referred to an agreement with the US on a licence.Since coming to office, Trump has scaled back direct military aid for Ukraine. Instead, Ukraine's European allies have been buying expensive US supplies - such as Patriot missiles - which are then donated to Ukraine."Ukraine does not have, nor will it ever have, the sort of funds that Russia has, which it is using to finance the war," Zelensky said on Saturday. "We have what we need, thanks to European aid and support from other countries. But additional funding specifically for Ukrainian production is what is needed."Earlier in the week, Zelensky said the supply of interceptors from allies had been "significantly reduced" this year.The Ukrainian leader was speaking during his first trip to Serbia.

articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin batters Japan's Okinawa before bearing down on China
articles.excerpt: Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday.Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived.The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes.Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival.The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country.Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said.Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot.

articles.title: US offers $1bn to Colombia on new right-wing president's first day of office
articles.excerpt: The US has pledged $1bn (£740m) to Colombia hours after the country's new right-wing populist president was sworn in.Abelardo de la Espriella, an admirer of Donald Trump who echoed many of the US president's policies on the campaign trail, used his maiden speech to promise an "all-out war" on drug cartels.The US state department said the "security package" would help him achieve "our shared goals", which include fighting organised crime and illegal immigration.

articles.title: Thai PM vows to introduce stricter gun laws after eight killed in shooting
articles.excerpt: Image source, EPAImage caption, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has pledged to introduce stricter gun lawsThailand's prime minister has vowed to introduce new gun control laws following a shooting by a teenager on the outskirts of Bangkok that left eight people dead and 22 injured.Fourteen people remain in hospital, seven of whom are in a critical condition. The 14-year-old killed his grandparents at the home they shared before travelling to Debsirin School in Nonthaburi, where he had been a student. There, he killed five teachers before taking his own life. Later, Thai media reported that a student had also died from their injuries.Speaking after the attack, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he planned to introduce laws that restrict the carrying of firearms in public.The new legislation will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns.Police Col Thadsakorn Konthong said that the gun and bullets used in the attack belonged to the teen's grandfather, with an initial inspection finding signs that the firearm had been searched for inside the grandfather's bedroom. International and local media have reported that the gun was legally registered and had a permit.Thailand has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in South East Asia, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, around four million of which are believed to be owned illegally.The country has strict gun laws, which punish the illegal possession of arms with up to 10 years in jail, but enforcement of these laws has been an issue.During his time as interior minister, Anutin introduced a number of gun control laws, including a short-term ban on new gun licenses and import restrictions.Speaking on Friday, the prime minister said the tragedy "shouldn't have happened"."I don't just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence pact
articles.excerpt: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a joint defence agreement, saying an attack on one of them would be seen as an attack on all three.The pact was announced at a meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in the Saudi city of Mecca.After the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Tehran and its allies struck targets in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil shipping channel, and the Red Sea.The Mecca agreement has drawn a sharp reaction from Tehran, where an senior member of parliament said it would not help Saudi Arabia."The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan does not bring them security, just as years of unilateral milking of the Americans did not bring them security," Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of National Security commission, wrote on his X.Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already announced a joint defence pact last year.The new Mecca Joint Defence Agreement sees three of the world's most powerful Muslim nations come together to offer mutual defence guarantees.It aims "to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all", a joint statement reads."It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defence co-operation among the three States."Although the pact pledges mutual support, it provides no specifics on the obligations of each party.

articles.title: Spanish police arrest 78 people in bust of 'one of largest' smuggling networks
articles.excerpt: One of the largest criminal networks smuggling drugs and people in the western Mediterranean has been dismantled, authorities have said.Europol said 78 people were arrested in Spain and Algeria in a bust of the network, that is also linked to other criminal activities including "violent robberies, extortion, illegal detentions, and money laundering".The group moved synthetic drugs from Spain and Portugal to Algeria, then used the return journey to smuggle migrants and weapons to the Spanish mainland and island of Ibiza on "ghost speedboats".Some of the items seized included 18 high-speed vessels valued at €5m (£4.2m), guns, more than €25,000 (£21,400) in cash and 15,000 MDMA pills.The sting, led by Spanish police, involved searches in 17 locations in Spain, including Alicante, Almería, Cartagena and Murcia.Europol said the group had "evolved from drug trafficking into a duel-flow criminal enterprise designed to maximise profits" with outbound routes from Spain and Portugal to Algeria. "The smuggling focused on synthetic drugs (such as MDMA), firearms, and explosives. Along routine routes from Algeria to Spain, the group smuggled migrants, charging up to €12,000 (£10,200) per person," Europol's statement said."In just one trip, over 50 migrants could be smuggled. All in all, profits from migrant smuggling alone are estimated to be more than €24m (£20m)." The network also provided services to other organised crime groups, "facilitating the movement of illicit goods and people across the Western Mediterranean". "Investigators believe the network coordinated multiple trafficking flows. Synthetic drugs, and sometimes people, were moved from France and Spain to Algeria, while cannabis resin, weapons, and migrants were transported from Algeria to Spain."Often, the group used a fleet of high-powered speedboats to conduct rapid maritime operations.

articles.title: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
articles.excerpt: Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, A former apprentice stonemason who helped build the Houses of Parliament is thought to have borrowed the book in the late 1800sByLana LamSydneyA book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London.Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s.The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member.Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia.Image source, Kiama CouncilImage caption, The book was a little water damaged but otherwise in a good conditionSimmons, a self-confessed family history buff, said his great-grandfather studied in London between 1839 to 1844."After his studies in London, he was apprenticed to other stonemasons to help in the construction of the Houses of Parliament," Simmons said.In 1857, aged 27, John Simmons emigrated from the UK to Australia, first living in the Sydney suburb of Newtown before relocating to Kiama after leading the construction of a sandstone church in the coastal town."He had quite an interest in architecture, construction and building," Simmons said, adding that the overdue book "probably sat on a shelf at his house" and was used as a reference.The book somehow ended up in a tea chest - along with other family records - which was placed in a fireplace that was covered up.Image source, Supplied: Jo HartmannImage caption, The fireplace where the book was found had been sealed for decadesAbout 30 years ago, the tea chest was uncovered during renovations and the books - including the overdue one - were

articles.title: Kidnapped rare Serbian eagle freed into wild after rescue
articles.excerpt: A rare eastern imperial eagle has been rescued from animal traffickers and released back into the wild in Serbia after months in captivity.After leaving the nest last year, Feliks was caught in Syria by poachers who eventually demanded a ransom - which was refused.After protracted talks the bird was taken to a wildlife centre in Beirut, Lebanon, where he recuperated for more than half a year before his repatriation on a Serbian military plane.The protected species is critically endangered, but conservation work since 2017 has brought the population in Serbia from one pair up to 29 pairs this year, according to the Bird Protection and Study Society of Serbia (BPSSS).In July 2025, just as the young raptor first flew the nest, experts tracked him for conservation purposes as he flew towards the Middle East."At that point, we started to worry because we could see that he was heading towards an extremely unsafe region," Uros Stojiljkovic of the BPSSS told the AFP news agency.When the bird's tracking signal was lost in October, initially it was thought the tracker was faulty.But it soon became clear Feliks had been abducted and eventually was put up for sale by poachers.

articles.title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
articles.excerpt: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts."I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced.

articles.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
articles.excerpt: ByTiffanie TurnbullReporting fromDryandra, Western Australia"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain.As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Dryandra Woodland is one of the few places you can still find wild numbatsAustralia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species.

articles.title: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketer
articles.excerpt: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketerImage source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib replaced Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the series against Sri Lanka beginning 15 AugustByMohsin KamalCricket writer"You play with so many cricket stars. Why don't you take selfies with them?"Bilal Ahmad Dar once asked his young cousin, Auqib Nabi.Auqib smiled and replied: "One day I will reach a place where they will want to take selfies with me."Years later, that prediction has come true.On Monday, the 29-year-old all-rounder became the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up after replacing Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka, which starts on 15 August.For a region where conflict, harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted sporting opportunities, Auqib's selection is being seen as a landmark moment.Raised in a small village in Baramulla district, Auqib grew up playing on local grounds with little infrastructure and few opportunities. His father, Ghulam Nabi Dar, a schoolteacher, initially wanted him to concentrate on academics and become a doctor.Image source, Abid BhatImage caption, Harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted cricket in Kashmir"There was no scope in cricket. We used to think playing sport was a waste of time, so I insisted that Auqib focused on his studies," Ghulam says.But Auqib's persistence eventually changed his father's mind."After seeing his passion for cricket, I accepted it. I realised that, as a parent and a teacher, I shouldn't force him to do something he didn't want to do. I started supporting him."Auqib's childhood friend, Junaid Dar, remembers growing up in an environment where professional cricket barely seemed possible."Auqib was obsessed with cricket from childhood. I used to ask him, 'Why are you doing all this?

articles.title: Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
articles.excerpt: Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task."Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.The state government has spent approximately 1m

articles.title: The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
articles.excerpt: At one time, Luka's own phone number was hard to avoid - in the early days of the Syrian civil war, it had been spray-painted on walls around the central city of Homs.The conflict was sparked by Assad's brutal crushing of a pro-democracy uprising in 2011 - a war in which hundreds of thousands of people would go on to be killed.Luka was a local head of the Political Security Directorate, one of Assad's main intelligence agencies, and had been given the task of wresting the city from the rebels.At the time, rebel-held areas in Homs were under siege by the government, and residents were struggling to access food and medicine. Several people, including former rebel fighter Motaz al-Zaydi, told us they had resorted to eating rats.Al-Zaydi remembers Luka's name and phone number appearing on a wall in his neighbourhood, and said the message began to spread that those wanting to flee the fighting could phone the number for safe passage.Some are believed to have been granted safe transit out of the city by Luka, but others who called the number were never seen or heard from again, according to several people we spoke to, including al-Zaydi.Many told us they referred to Luka as "The Spider" because of his vast web of allies and informants, including some embedded in rebel groups. "He was everywhere," Homs residents told us. Al-Zaydi described Luka as an "evil genius" and "a fox of a man".But his most egregious action in the city, many argue, was his alleged involvement in the so-called Eid Massacre, known by some as the Children's Massacre, which the US noted when sanctioning him."They were tiny children," he said with tears in his eyes.

articles.title: Watch: Moment opposition MP throws eggs at Kosovo's acting PM
articles.excerpt: An opposition MP, Time Kadrijaj, threw eggs at Kosovo's acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti during a plenary session on Saturday. The Alliance party MP hurled at least four eggs in Kurti's direction before lawmakers and police officers intervened. Chaos unfolded after Kurti told Parliament he needed more time to hold talks with other parties before proposing a candidate for speaker following the June snap election.

articles.title: Watch: BBC asks Infantino if he will resign as Fifa president
articles.excerpt: The BBC has asked Fifa president Gianni Infantino if he has the support of football's South American governing body, Conmebol.The Fifa head has faced multiple calls to resign after his highly controversial attempt to sell private stakes in the World Cup, which he later abandoned.Infantino, who did not answer the BBC's questions, was in Colombia for the inauguration of the country's new President Abelardo de la Espriella.The BBC's South America correspondent Ione Wells later asked the Fifa president if he would step down.Read more: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

articles.title: What we know so far about the deadly Thailand shooting
articles.excerpt: At least seven people have died after a 14-year-old boy shot and killed his grandparents and then opened fire on a school in Thailand's capital, Bangkok.Authorities say the suspect, who was a student at the school, used a handgun belonging to his grandfather in the attacks, before turning the gun on himself. BBC South East Asia correspondent Jonathan Head reports from the school where the deadly shooting took place.More on this story.

articles.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
articles.excerpt: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.
