articles.title: Trump targets birthright citizenship again
articles.excerpt: NewsFeedUS President Donald Trump has signed two new executive orders targeting birthright citizenship, just weeks after the Supreme Court rejected his broader attempt to restrict it. This time, the administration is targeting so-called “birth tourism” and other categories of foreign nationals. Al Jazeera’s Noor Wazwaz explains.Published On 9 Aug 2026

articles.title: Israel’s ‘Green Rafah’ plan aims to fragment Gaza, experts say
articles.excerpt: Israel has quietly given the green light for infrastructure work to begin in a designated area of southern Gaza, according to Israeli media, as it advances a post-war vision that experts warn is designed to reshape reality on the ground and permanently fragment the enclave.Dubbed “Green Rafah”, the project backed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz is in eastern Rafah near the unilaterally imposed “Yellow Line”, the effective Israeli buffer zone squeezing Palestinians into smaller areas.Army Radio, which reported the approval on Sunday, said the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office described the initiative as an Emirati-backed pilot project aimed at establishing temporary housing “free” of the influence of the Palestinian group Hamas.While the Israeli military will reportedly supervise the installation of water, sewage and electrical infrastructure, Palestinian labourers will be subjected to intense security screenings by the Shin Bet intelligence agency.Furthermore, strict limitations have been imposed on the project, with Israeli authorities reportedly banning the entry of “caravans” or mobile homes into the area until at least November.Also on Sunday, Netanyahu said he rejects the 15-point plan for Gaza announced last month by the United States-led Board of Peace.The plan calls for the disarmament of Hamas in stages and the phased withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Strip, but Netanyahu said an Israeli pull-out won’t happen until Hamas is fully disarmed.As political negotiations over the future of Gaza stall, Palestinian political researcher Ahmed al-Atawneh warned that projects such as “Green Rafah” are designed to create isolated cantons under total Israeli administrative and security control.

articles.title: China’s Asian Affairs Reshuffle
articles.excerpt: On July 21, President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa awarded Shen Minjuan, China’s ambassador to the country since 2023, Mongolia’s Order of the Polar Star (Altangadas), the country’s highest state honor for foreign nationals. Barely a week later, on July 29, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) updated its official organizational roster: Shen had taken office as director-general of the Department of Asian Affairs, succeeding Liu Jinsong. The speed of the promotion was striking. So was its symbolism. For Mongolian policymakers and analysts who observed Shen’s nearly three-year tenure up close, her elevation to one of the most influential operational posts in Chinese foreign policy is more than a routine bureaucratic rotation. It is the clearest signal yet that Beijing is recalibrating its approach to its immediate periphery – moving away from the overtly assertive style that defined much of the past half-decade toward a more calibrated, geoeconomics-driven model. From a Mongolian vantage point, this adjustment makes eminent strategic sense for China. Years of so-called “wolf warrior diplomacy” have yielded diminishing returns across its neighborhood. A more unyielding diplomatic approach accelerated hedging behavior in Southeast Asia, deepened security coordination between Washington and its regional allies, and made it harder for smaller states to maintain the balanced, pragmatic relations most prefer. Shen’s record in Ulaanbaatar suggests she understands this dynamic. Her task now is to apply lessons learned in a relatively manageable bilateral setting to a vastly more complex regional portfolio. The vacancy she leaves behind in Mongolia – and who fills it – will offer an early clue as to how broadly this new approach is intended to apply. This recalibration has precedents.

articles.title: Hopes for the North Korean Human Rights Act of 2026
articles.excerpt: Since the COVID-19 border closures sealed North Korea off from the world, and as the China-Russia-North Korea axis has deepened, the North Korean people have become more isolated and vulnerable than at any point in recent memory. In this grim period, one piece of encouraging news stands out: last month, U.S. Senators Tim Kaine (D-VA) and Dan Sullivan (R-AK) introduced the bipartisan North Korean Human Rights Reauthorization Act (NKHRA). Growing up in North Korea, America was my enemy – alongside South Korea, the U.S. is one of the two principal adversaries the state taught us to despise. I was taught that American missionaries had pressed the word “thief” into an innocent boy’s forehead with caustic acid. We called Americans “wolf-like Yankee imperialists” and were told they sought to swallow the Korean peninsula whole. When I escaped in 2013, I carried that conditioning with me – until American volunteers with no family ties to North Korea, no personal stake, no obligation, wept and prayed alongside me for the family I had left behind. And as I slowly learned the truth about the outside world, I discovered something that humbled me entirely: the very government I had been raised to fear had passed the North Korean Human Rights Act in 2004, becoming the first country in the world to formally recognize that what was happening inside North Korea was not merely a political problem, but ongoing crimes against humanity. The Americans had been fighting for people they would never meet, in a country they were prohibited from entering, for decades. The North Korean Human Rights Act, or NKHRA, expired in 2022. On June 25, Senators Kane and Sullivan reintroduced the NKHRA, signaling Congress’s continued commitment to advancing the rights of the North Korean people. This effort to revive the NKHRA legislation is part of a long bipartisan tradition.

articles.title: India’s Climate Stress and the Solar Power Paradox
articles.excerpt: In April and May 2026, all of the 50 hottest cities in the world were located in India, an ominous distinction for the country, which is witnessing deep, systemic climate stress. This trend has continued unabated into subsequent months, with high temperatures and humidity levels driving increased use of cooling appliances such as air conditioners across many states in India. In July 2026, India’s electrical energy consumption grew 10.93 percent year-on-year to 170.70 billion units (BU). In comparison, the country’s total power consumption was 153.88 BU in July 2025. The peak power demand also jumped to 270.20 GW in July 2026. It was 220.74 GW in July 2025. The all-time record high was set in May this year with demand of 270.82 GW. The steep rise in temperature and heat waves may be a problem for people, but for the leading air conditioner manufacturers, it is a buoyant market. Companies like Voltas and LG Electronics have reported high sales. Each had already sold over 1 million units in the first three months of the year. Panasonic India said its residential AC sales increased by 50 percent year-on-year in the summer season of 2026, representing its highest-ever level. These are very high figures for a developing country, where 60 percent of the population depends on food subsidies and power bills are on a constant rise. It also demonstrates the fact that the rising middle class, not just in metros, but also in tier-two towns and beyond, is responding to the threat and discomfort of a warming climate with significant uptake of household cooling options. Access to air conditioning, seen increasingly as a significant health issue globally, also contributes to the global warming and climate crisis. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6 percent in 2026 and 3.8 percent in 2027, driven by industry, cooling, electric vehicles (EVs), and data centers.

articles.title: No Wonderland: Alice’s Shameful Australian Aboriginal Camps
articles.excerpt: Alice Springs, or “Alice” as it is commonly known here in Australia, is situated in the country’s Red Center. For over 30,000 years, the Arrernte Aboriginal people have been custodians of this remote land – a land of red earth, awe-inspiring rock formations and ethereal skies. Alice, or Mparntwe in the Arrernte language, has profound, unhealed wounds, both ancient and recent. The most recent, and still painfully raw, is the murder in late April of a 5-year-old girl. An Aboriginal man by the name of Jefferson Lewis has been charged with her murder. In accordance with Aboriginal custom, under which the names of the dead are avoided out of respect, the family requested she be called Kumanjayi Little Baby. She was found dead after disappearing from the Aboriginal Old Timers Camp, one of the 18 Aboriginal camps on the fringes of Alice Springs. Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family were staying in a dilapidated house at the Old Timers Camp after traveling from their remote community in the Tanami Desert to Alice Springs to access medical care. Photos taken at the Old Timers Camp during the search for the girl showed a mattress on the floor where she had been put to bed before her disappearance. Police said Jefferson Lewis, the alleged killer of Kumanjayi Little Baby, was staying at the Old Timers Camp too.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Missing Deterrent
articles.excerpt: Deterrence has been a consistent national priority for Taiwan amid the intensifying pressure from China, which frames reunification with Taiwan as an essential component to the Chinese Communist Party’s goal of national rejuvenation, nominally targeted for 2049. Taiwan’s deterrence strategy relies heavily on U.S. arms sales, security assistance, and military technology cooperation. Conventional deterrents are necessary: F-16V fighters, Indigenous Defense Fighters, and Patriot missile systems prevent adversarial air superiority; Hsiung Feng anti-ship missiles, sea mines, and Harpoon Coastal Defense Systems repel amphibious invasions; ground forces and HIMARS batteries help blunt, endure, and counter an initial attack. Conventional capabilities are acquired and designed to make military advances prohibitively costly for China. However, conventional deterrence alone overlooks the vector of conflict most likely to define a cross-strait crisis: civil defense. Chinese tactics in economic coercion are well-documented, Taiwan’s submarine cable network remains vulnerable to sabotage, and Beijing maintains a cognitive warfare apparatus designed to disinform and manipulate Taiwanese public opinion. These challenges cannot be dealt with purely militarily; they require robust civil defense that resists unconventional ruptures to the continuity of life and develops societal preparedness to withstand crises. The establishment of the All-Out Defense Mobilization Agency, the introduction of “whole-of-society resilience” in official rhetoric, and civilian resources pointed at a military invasion illustrate how civil defense is prioritized within Taiwan’s defense strategy. Yet, Taiwan’s current civil defense capabilities remain insufficient due to fragmented preparedness initiatives, uneven civil-military coordination, and domestic political stagnation.

articles.title: China’s Military Is Now Using AI to Plan Strike Operations
articles.excerpt: The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force now uses an AI system that draws up plans for large-scale strike operations. Instead of being released with great fanfare, the system appeared in a CCTV documentary released in early August to mark the PLA’s 99th anniversary. The system is described as prioritizing targets from a pool of hundreds, coordinating dozens of formations, and assigning tasks to more than 100 tactical units. According to the documentary, it has already been used in multiple missions. The timing lines up neatly with Xi Jinping’s instruction in late July that the PLA must strengthen the military application of unmanned intelligent technologies and gradually build an intelligent military system. As China has been pursuing this very goal for years, Xi’s remarks are not new. The level of emphasis, however, is high: Beijing wants steady progress toward the modernization goals set for 2027, which marks the 100th anniversary of the PLA’s founding. The AI system is described to handle a volume of decisions that would otherwise overwhelm human planners as, so goes the argument, traditional calculation methods cannot keep up when large numbers of aircraft and targets move at high speed. This indeed is a fair assessment and is far from being unique to China. Unlike autonomous weapon systems, the software does not select and engage targets directly. Its significance lies higher in the command chain. It helps plan air campaigns by recommending how aircraft, electronic warfare assets, and supporting capabilities should be combined before commanders authorize execution. In other words the system is described as a support tool that helps commanders and pilots – but humans remain responsible for the final decisions. As is often the case with great powers and military AI, there is a catch in China’s posture and the potential operation realities.

articles.title: How China Is Reordering Global Governance From Within
articles.excerpt: On June 17, the State Council Information Office published “More Just and Equitable Global Governance: China’s Principles, Proposals and Actions.” Its most revealing line was also its most conservative: “All countries should firmly uphold the international system with the U.N. at its core, safeguard the international order based on international law, and uphold the basic norms governing international relations underpinned by the purposes and principles of the U.N. Charter, instead of reinventing the wheel.” On July 16, 29 governments signed the founding agreement of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) in Shanghai. The new body, headquartered in China, invokes the United Nations Charter and a “people-centered” approach. Together, these two events capture Beijing’s method for remaking global governance. Rather than propose a rival constitution, China preserves the institutions and texts of the postwar order while reweighting their principles and creating new, China-led venues to operationalize them. China’s visions stresses sovereign equality, noninterference, state-led development, and negotiated consent gain weight; independent scrutiny, adverse judgment, and claims beyond governmental mediation all recede. Reform Without Rupture Looking for a “status quo” or a “revisionist” China sets up the wrong binary. As Alastair Iain Johnston argued, there is no single international order that a state accepts or rejects; China takes different positions toward issue-specific orders. Beijing calls this “reform,” and the new white paper shows what it looks like in practice. China’s President Xi Jinping launched the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus meeting in Tianjin on September 1, 2025. Its concept paper identified three deficits: Global South underrepresentation, weakened rules, and institutional ineffectiveness on development and new domains such as artificial intelligence.

articles.title: India’s Communal Violence is Crossing into Nepal
articles.excerpt: Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh region abutting India appears increasingly prone to religious strife. With the sway of India’s Hindu nationalist groups like the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) steadily building on Nepali soil, the country is also witnessing more Hindu-Muslim tensions. While common in north India, such incidents had been rare in Nepal until recently. Earlier this month, four Nepali youths were killed in clashes with police. The immediate cause of the incident was a Hindu procession passing through Dewanjung in Sunsari district, blasting loud music. The local Muslims protested. A clash ensued, police intervened and three youths were killed. (A fourth died in related protests in another district.) Local accounts suggest the Hindus in the area were already angry as the organizers of Muharram — a festival that marks the start of the Islamic calendar — had yet to remove some green pennants planted for the festival a month before. According to one newspaper investigation, there were at least 17 such incidents of Hindu-Muslim tensions in the Tarai belt in the past eight years. Earlier, Nepali Hindus seldom felt the need to publicly assert their religious identity. But as the Hindu forces in India started the rather brazen display of anti-Muslim activities starting in the early 1990s — most infamous of which was the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya — the observation of Hindu festivals and rituals also began to change in Nepal. By the time of the inauguration of the Ram Temple in India’s Ayodhya in January 2024, rooftop saffron flags had become a common sight in Hindu homes in the Tarai-Madhesh. As religious identities became more publicly politicized, saffron flags were increasingly answered by green pennants in Muslim households. Again emulating practices across the border, elaborate religious processions accompanied by loud music also became common among Nepali Hindus and Muslims alike.

articles.title: From Jobs to Skills: Rethinking Vietnam’s FDI success
articles.excerpt: Vietnam attracted $34.65 billion in registered foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first half of 2026, 61 percent more than the same period in 2025. At the same time, realized FDI reached $13.03 billion, its highest first-half level in five years. Observers including Harvard’s Growth Lab have also pointed to Vietnam’s increasingly diverse and sophisticated export base as a source of strong long-run growth prospects. By conventional measures, the country’s development model is working. Despite this, another important labor-market signal has been moving in the opposite direction. Since the late 2000s, the wage premium earned by staying in school has been falling, with particularly marked falls for university graduates. This does not necessarily mean that education has become less valuable in itself. It may instead mean that the economy is not creating enough jobs that make productive use of advanced skills. Whatever the reality, it has important implications for the Vietnamese government’s ambition of reaching high-income status by 2045. The gains from moving workers out of agriculture and into factories and services cannot continue indefinitely; future growth requires sustained productivity growth rather than labor reallocation alone. So far, Vietnam’s FDI model has succeeded on employment quantity but underperformed on occupational upgrading. Drawing on 13 years of nationally representative Labor Force Survey data, a recent study that we conducted found that for every 100 jobs created in foreign-invested firms, an additional 100 jobs emerge in the same district – a local employment multiplier of roughly one to one. This is a large spillover, and a compelling reason why FDI has become such a central part of Vietnam’s growth story. Foreign firms accounted for around one-tenth of total employment in 2023, up from almost nothing before 2000. Factory jobs raise household incomes and local spending, creating employment in other businesses.

articles.title: Thailand Pledges to Work Towards Myanmar’s Full Reintegration With ASEAN
articles.excerpt: Thailand has affirmed its intention to bring Myanmar back into the ASEAN fold, following a meeting between Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and the country’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, in Bangkok yesterday. The summit was the highlight of the former general’s two-day visit to Thailand, his first official visit to the country since he led a military coup in 2021. After arriving in Bangkok, Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome by Anutin, who then hosted him for talks at Government House in Bangkok. During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing also attended an official dinner, met the leaders of both houses of the Thai parliament, and spoke at a Thai-Myanmar business forum in the Thai capital, before departing today. In a joint statement issued late yesterday, Thailand “reaffirmed its commitment to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.” Myanmar in turn “expressed its appreciation for Thailand’s constructive role in facilitating the normalization of its relations with ASEAN.” In the statement, the two countries said they agreed to “further deepen dialogue at all levels,” in the areas of security, trade, and environmental protection. They also expressed their “joint commitment to achieve a peaceful and stable Thailand–Myanmar border.” The visit saw the signing of three bilateral deals between the two nations. As per Nikkei Asia, these included an agreement on Burmese migrant labor in Thailand and another setting up a joint working group to address river pollution from rare-earth mining. The two leaders also reportedly discussed ways to boost cross-border trade, including the resumption of trade over the Second Friendship Bridge connecting the Thai town of Mae Sot with Myawaddy in eastern Myanmar.

articles.title: How the World Learned to Live with the Exclusion of Afghan Women
articles.excerpt: Five years ago, when the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, the world watched in shock as images emerged of desperate Afghans trying to escape a country whose future had suddenly changed. For Afghan women and girls, however, the fall of Afghanistan was the beginning of a systematic effort to remove them from public life and rob an entire generation of their future. Today, girls have been banned from secondary schools and universities; women have been pushed out of workplaces; and restrictions on movement, expression, and participation in society have expanded. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are prohibited from accessing secondary and higher education. More than 2 million adolescent girls have been denied their right to continue learning. But five years later, the most troubling question is how the world learned to live with the Taliban’s policies toward women and girls. Since August 2021, the language surrounding Afghanistan has changed. After the Taliban takeover, the world demanded the restoration of the rights of Afghan women and girls. Five years later, much of the conversation has shifted toward how to engage with the Taliban while raising concerns about women’s rights. The U.N. and other international community actors have adopted a policy of “principled engagement,” arguing that dialogue is needed to address Afghanistan’s humanitarian crisis while continuing to call for an end to restrictions on women and girls. Engagement and diplomacy are complicated realities. Afghanistan is facing a humanitarian crisis, and millions of Afghans depend on international assistance. But there is a dangerous line between engaging with a country’s oppressive regime and allowing the systematic exclusion of half the population to become normalized. Consequently, the Taliban’s strategy has focused on waiting for global attention to its treatment of women to decline.

articles.title: Where Is Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi?
articles.excerpt: Beyond the Mekong | Politics | Southeast Asia Sean Turnell, an economist and former advisor to the ousted leader, returns to Beyond The Mekong to discuss recent events in Myanmar. The military-backed government in Myanmar this week released four photos of the country’s jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who met with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, on August 3. “This may be a first step, but it must not be the last,” her son, Kim Aris, said in a statement. Sean Turnell, an Australian economist who worked with Suu Kyi and then shared a prison with her after the military coup in 2021, agrees, adding that “proof of life” is also required for some 20,000 people who are believed to be held as political prisoners inside Myanmar’s jails. Turnell returned to Beyond the Mekong and spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about the first confirmation of Suu Kyi’s existence in many years and the issues facing the opposition National Unity Government (NUG) and the various armed groups battling the military. The NUG, its People’s Defense Force (PDF), and the country’s numerous ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) have faced a resurgent military this year and a counter-offensive aimed at retaking territory won by the rebels during 2023 and 2024. Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader and now military-backed civilian leader, has also gone on a diplomatic offensive in search of international legitimacy for his administration within ASEAN, which wants the junta to return to its Five-Point Consensus as a roadmap for peace. Turnell, who spent 650 days behind bars prior to his release in November 2022, says the civil war, which has claimed some 100,000 lives, cannot be won by the military, as the NUG and EAOs continue to formulate a federal framework for a country mired by ethnic differences. But eventually, he says, peace will prevail.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Top Leader To Lam to Pay State Visits to Australia and New Zealand
articles.excerpt: Vietnam’s President To Lam will next week embark on state visits to Australia and New Zealand, the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday. In a statement, it announced that Lam, who also serves as general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), would travel to the two nations from August 9 to 14, but did not specify the exact itinerary. The trip, which has been rumored for several weeks, was confirmed by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s office, which said that Lam would be in Australia on August 9-12 and would meet with Albanese on August 11 in order “to discuss opportunities to deepen cooperation.” “I look forward to welcoming General Secretary and President To Lam to Australia and discussing how we can strengthen cooperation between our two nations,” Albanese said in the statement. “The Vietnam-Australia relationship is grounded in deep strategic trust, mutual interests, and a shared ambition for the future of our region.” The New Zealand government also confirmed that Lam would arrive in Auckland on August 12 and depart the following day. The Vietnamese leader’s trip to Australia is likely to build on the momentum created by the two nations’ establishment of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in March 2024. This raised Australia to the highest tier of Vietnam’s diplomatic hierarchy, alongside Russia, China, and the United States, and pledged to develop “all aspects of our relationship,” including defense and security, trade, education, energy cooperation, and digital transformation. Lam’s visit, his first to Australia since being appointed president in April, will “consolidate political trust at the highest level and provide fresh momentum for the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership,” Vietnam’s Ambassador to Australia Pham Hung Tam told state media.

articles.title: Japan’s Billions Are the Wildcard in Southeast Asia’s Aid Race
articles.excerpt: For the last two decades, the contest for influence in Southeast Asia has almost always been conceptualized as a two-horse race: China floods the region with infrastructure loans and the United States counters with democracy programs and health assistance. This binary framing obscures the presence of a third player, one whose role may prove more decisive than either Washington or Beijing: Japan. For decades, Tokyo has without fanfare underwritten much of Southeast Asia’s development. According to the Lowy Institute’s 2025 Southeast Asia Aid Map, Japan disbursed around $35 billion in development finance to the region between 2015 and 2023. This is less than China’s $50 billion in actual disbursements, but far more than the United States’ $9 billion. More critically, Japan’s assistance arrives as grants and concessional loans governed by transparent standards, governance principles, and environmental safeguards. In official development finance share for 2022, Japan (30 percent) and the Western bloc combined (31 percent) still outpaced China (24 percent) across Southeast Asia, a fact routinely drowned out by headlines announcing each new Belt and Road mega-project. Japan’s dominance in the region’s development landscape is not new. For much of the post-war era, Tokyo has treated its overseas development assistance (ODA) as a strategic instrument linking infrastructure to trade expansion and the cultivation of stable bilateral ties. The Fukuda Doctrine of 1977 institutionalized this commitment, resulting in decades of accumulated trust. That trust is now being tested. Since 2013, China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has dramatically reshuffled regional development finance. Beijing has committed approximately $149 billion to Southeast Asia, concentrating flows overwhelmingly in transport and energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Was Tarique Rahman’s Youth Outreach More Than an Election Strategy?
articles.excerpt: After 17 years in exile, Tarique Rahman, then acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), returned to Dhaka on December 25, 2025. By then, people’s political aspirations had changed significantly through a mass uprising and political transition following a long period of authoritarian rule. In the aftermath of the July 2024 uprising, Bangladesh’s youth had moved to the center of politics. They not only led the movement that brought down Sheikh Hasina’s government, but also made up a significant portion of the electorate that would choose the next. The youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP) emerged in the political arena; most of its leaders had been at the forefront of the July uprising. Ahead of the national election, Jamaat-e-Islami, in alliance with the NCP and several other Islamist parties, was mounting a political challenge. Rahman and his party did not take long to recognize the reality. After returning home, he placed young people at the center of various programs, policy plans, and the party’s election manifesto. During the election campaign, several events were organized exclusively for the youth. At that time, analysts viewed them as part of the BNP’s strategy to attract young voters. The formal campaign for Bangladesh’s 13th parliamentary election began on January 22 this year. On that day, Rahman was in Sylhet, a city around 250 kilometers from Dhaka. He attended an event titled “The Plan: Youth Policy Talk with Tarique Rahman,” where several hundred students from different educational institutions heard the leader of the country’s largest political party explain his plans for nation-building. The students also shared their views and raised questions. Rahman responded to them and sought their suggestions. A similar event was later held in Chattogram. He also engaged directly with the youth through other programs. The BNP’s election manifesto contained many promises for the youth.

articles.title: How South Korea Can Survive the Unbundling of International Order
articles.excerpt: For most of the post-war era, power, legitimacy, and cooperation reinforced one another. American leadership underwrote security, open markets, and freedom of navigation. Democratic partnerships generated political trust. Universal institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, and the nuclear nonproliferation regime provided common rules and legal legitimacy. Though imperfect, these three pillars generally worked in concert. That alignment has broken down. Security, economic governance, political legitimacy, and practical cooperation are no longer occurring in the same institutions or even among the same groups of states. I call this structural transformation the “unbundling of order.” The result is disalignment, a condition in which power, legitimacy, and cooperation no longer reinforce one another. Analysts today often ask whether the liberal international order is collapsing or which great power will replace the United States. The real question is whether the essential functions of the international order can be reconnected under increasingly fragmented geopolitical conditions. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed the inability of existing institutions like the United Nations to prevent or halt great power aggression. The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran demonstrated that military superiority alone cannot ensure regional stability or the credibility of the global nonproliferation regime. Competition – especially, but not exclusively between China and the United States – over semiconductors, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, and maritime supply chains blurs the traditional boundary between economics and security. Cooperation is increasingly necessary, but the most inclusive institutions are often the least capable of collective action. This paradox has driven the rise of minilateralism.

articles.title: The Rule of Law in Afghanistan Failed Long Before the Taliban’s Triumph
articles.excerpt: Nearly five years after Taliban insurgents toppled the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, calls still ring out for a return to the rule of law. United Nations officials contend that Taliban governance “precipitated the collapse of the rule of law and judicial independence in Afghanistan.” Amnesty International pleads for the Taliban to “reinstate a formal constitutional and legal framework and the rule of law.” The idea that Afghanistan lost the rule of law in 2021 is compelling. It is also a fantasy. The United States, and the international community more broadly, abandoned rule of law in Afghanistan long before the Taliban returned. The U.S.-backed regime that the Taliban defeated was one of the most corrupt states on Earth. And within that regime, police and courts were consistently ranked among the most corrupt parts. For example, a major 2018 survey found “corruption within the local security and justice sector in Afghanistan remains a key driver of insecurity in the country.” The United States’ willingness to not only tolerate but also perpetuate corruption and lawlessness proved essential for the Taliban’s success. What of the U.S. role? Here, too, reality and rhetoric clash. Government officials and outside commentators routinely stress the idea that progress in law and justice was occurring and would have continued. As my recent work in Law & Social Inquiry shows, this is not the case. Trying and Failing At first, the U.S. envisioned the new Islamic Republic of Afghanistan as committed to the rule of law. Yet, initial efforts were outsourced to Italy and achieved little. Worse still, they backed a strong presidency and an unrepresentative parliamentary system that offered a decidedly weak foundation for a state built on the rule of law. As the Taliban insurgency gathered strength in the mid 2000s, Afghan government corruption became a key concern. Courts were expensive, unprofessional, predatory, and generally ineffective.

articles.title: Bangladesh-India Relations Hit Fresh Turbulence
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has said she will return to her country in December this year, almost two and a half years after fleeing to India following violent student protests that culminated in the ouster of her government. In a message delivered online to Indian and foreign journalists in New Delhi on August 5, Hasina said her decision to return home was based on her desire to serve her country and its people. Acknowledging the possibility of imprisonment or even execution if she returned to Bangladesh, Hasina said that such apprehensions would not deter her. “My return, and the return of the Awami League to the democratic process, is not about power. It is about putting Bangladesh back on the right track,” Hasina said. She also defended her government’s action against protesters who she said had destroyed public infrastructure and vandalized monuments associated with Sheikh Mujibur Rehman, who led Bangladesh’s liberation war in 1971 and became independent Bangladesh’s first president. Hasina’s media interaction drew an angry response from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party government, which expressed “outrage” over India allowing the press conference to be organized in Delhi. “Dhaka deeply regrets that in spite of concerns conveyed a priori to the Government of India about the likely ramifications of this event on the reset of our bilateral relations, this public event was permitted to be held,” it said. That it took place on the very day that Bangladesh was observing the second anniversary of Hasina’s ouster was “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution,” it added. On the eve of Hasina’s online interaction with the media, India distanced itself from the Hasina event, saying it had no role in it nor had it endorsed it. The Awami League presser was hosted by the Foreign Correspondents Club of South Asia in New Delhi. But that did not convince Bangladesh.

articles.title: Clashes Erupt at Susta Along India-Nepal Border
articles.excerpt: The long-standing India-Nepal dispute over Susta, one of the most geographically and politically sensitive sections of the Nepal-India border, erupted in violent clashes on August 2 between Nepali villagers and Indian border security personnel. The latter had allegedly crossed into Nepali territory in Nawalparasi West and dismantled an under-construction embankment built by local residents to prevent flooding. Nepal’s Armed Police Force had to intervene to prevent further escalation. According to Nepali media, a similar iincident happened in June, when India’s Border Security Force personnel entered an embankment construction site in Susta Municipality-5 and pressured workers to halt the project, which was part of ongoing efforts to provide protection for flood-prone settlements in the area. India is yet to respond officially to these allegations. India and Nepal share a 1,800-km-long open border. Susta in southern Nepal and the Kalapani-Limpiyadhura-Lipulekh area to Nepal’s west are disputed. With regard to the dispute over Susta, there are no boundary pillars along the 24-km stretch of this region, and India and Nepal rely on natural features such as rivers and trees to mark the boundary. The shifting course of the Gandak (also known as Narayani) river, the midstream of which formed the boundary under the Treaty of Sugauli of 1816, has further complicated the border problem here. Citing official sources from Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Nepali media publication reported that the Nepali Embassy in New Delhi raised Sunday’s clashes at Susta with India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) immediately. India’s position, according to this source, was that since the area where the embankment was built is disputed, the construction violates the “status quo” maintained between the two countries. India’s MEA is yet to issue a comment on this incident.

articles.title: China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law is Already Harming Uyghurs
articles.excerpt: China’s new Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress has been in effect for more than one month. Beijing claims the law will foster cohesion and protect the rights of minorities. In reality, it is already doing the opposite. One month in, the law is already harming Uyghurs and other ethnic groups and dissidents. Governments must take decisive action to challenge the law and protect diaspora communities before it is too late. As numerous sources have warned, the new law codifies a dramatic shift away from even the promise of regional autonomy, instead embedding Xi Jinping’s campaign of forced assimilation into nearly every facet of government and public life. In doing so, the law violates China’s own constitution. For Uyghurs, this is not new. In 2017, a Chinese official summarized the government’s strategy toward Uyghurs: “Break their lineage, break their roots, break their connections, and break their origins.” Since then, Chinese authorities have systematically dismantled Uyghur social, cultural, and religious life in what the United States government and numerous national parliaments have formally recognized as genocide and crimes against humanity. The indoctrination Uyghurs faced in internment camps, where authorities sought to replace Islam and Uyghur identity with loyalty to the CCP, is now imposed in daily life across the Uyghur homeland of East Turkestan. What has changed is this: Government actions that could once be described as regional campaigns are now embedded in national legislation. These restrictions will become easier to expand and harder to challenge.

articles.title: Balochistan Is Now Pakistan’s Most Dangerous Province
articles.excerpt: Balochistan witnessed an unprecedented surge in separatist violence in July: 176 terrorist attacks, involving suicide bombings, complex ambushes, coordinated high-profile assaults and drone operations, were reported that month, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal’s open-source database. In total, the attacks killed 438 people, including 127 security personnel. July was the most violent month in Balochistan this year, both in terms of attacks and fatalities. The statistics make Balochistan Pakistan’s most volatile province, surpassing Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where 143 violent incidents caused 244 casualties the same month. The data trendlines of terrorist attacks and killings so far in 2026 also reveal that Balochistan has overtaken Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the most volatile region in the country. As compared to 574 attacks and 1,196 casualties reported in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa between January and July this year, Balochistan witnessed a staggering 765 violent incidents and 1,600 fatalities in the same period. In addition to the increase in the number of terrorist attacks is the geographic expansion of violence to Balochistan’s Pashtun areas, where Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) has been quietly increasing its footprint. The TTP unleashed its firepower on former personnel of the Afghan National Army (ANA), who have been reorganizing and rearming in the province to relaunch the anti-Taliban campaign in Afghanistan. Ironically, ex-ANA factions are using the same residential compounds where once the Taliban’s Quetta shura lived, trained, and launched insurgent campaigns in Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban have tasked the TTP to counter the presence of ex-ANA elements in Balochistan’s Pashtun areas. Recent clashes between the TTP and ex-ANA elements have resulted in casualties among Pashtuns in Balochistan, prompting Pashtun tribes in Balochistan to protest, demanding justice and security from the state.

articles.title: Delhi’s EV Policy Changes the Engine, Not the System
articles.excerpt: At a traffic signal in Delhi, an electric SUV can wait beside an e-rickshaw and a delivery worker on an electric scooter. All three may be counted as evidence of the same green transition, although they embody very different relationships to mobility. The SUV offers private comfort and status; the e-rickshaw provides shared transport; the scooter is often inseparable from a worker’s livelihood. To see only three electric vehicles here is to miss the differences in power and vulnerability. This is what technological optimism does: treats a change in the machine as if it were automatically a transformation of the system. Delhi’s new Electric Vehicles Policy, notified on June 30, and effective from July 1, 2026, is nevertheless a serious intervention. From January 2027, only electric three-wheelers and N1-category light goods vehicles can be newly registered; from April 2028, the mandate extends to new two-wheelers. First-year purchase incentives reach 30,000 Indian rupees for electric two-wheelers, and 50,000 rupees for e-autos. Electric cars priced up to 3 million rupees receive road-tax and registration-fee exemptions, while eligible owners who scrap older cars can receive 100,000 rupees. The policy also supports charging, battery recycling and government electric buses. Unlike India’s national PM E-DRIVE scheme, though, the new policy combines incentives with mandatory deadlines. The policy identified vehicles as contributing 23 percent of Delhi’s winter air pollution and noted that two-wheelers constitute about 67 percent of its vehicle stock. Prioritizing intensively used two- and three-wheelers, goods vehicles, and buses is sensible. EVs eliminate tailpipe exhaust, use energy more efficiently, and generally produce lower lifecycle emissions than comparable petrol or diesel vehicles.

articles.title: Mongolia’s Fuel Crisis Is a Demand Problem, Not Just a Supply One
articles.excerpt: As Mongolians prepare for the back-to-school season while tourists prepare for long road trips, the transportation sector is in limbo. Long lines of cars wait for hours for fuel, sometimes to find no fuel at all. The government was forced to impose restrictions on fuel sales by limiting the maximum amount that can be purchased on select days. The cause of the crisis can be attributed to both external geopolitical factors and internal country dynamics, highlighting Mongolia’s ongoing energy insecurity. The cure might be a path toward transportation electrification. While Mongolia has proven crude oil deposits, the country is solely dependent on imported fuel, with 97 percent of it coming from Russia. The war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East are creating instability in global energy systems, which could impact the supply side. However, despite the popular notion of delays in Russian fuel shipments to Mongolia, sources have not cited any “major” delays from Russia, which makes it harder to pinpoint the cause of the current situation. Internally, urbanization and a mining boom in Mongolia have pushed demand higher, by up to 14 percent annually. For instance, Mongolia imported roughly 500,000 tonnes of petrol and diesel fuel in 2005; however, this number jumped five times higher within 20 years, reaching close to 2.7 million tonnes in 2025. The strategic vulnerability caused by Mongolia’s fuel dependency is a well-established fact within energy security calculus. The government has been pursuing a diversification plan, including talks with Kazakhstan on fuel imports and, more recently, with South Korea. Last week, Mongolian Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources Damdinnyam Gongor was in South Korea, striking deals on petroleum products. The country is expected to receive the first batch of diesel, petroleum, and aviation fuel from South Korea as soon as this month, according to the Government of Mongolia’s social media page.

articles.title: How Kazakhstan Wrote Its Security Service Into the AI Business
articles.excerpt: Securitization of digital infrastructure is not new, nor is the involvement of national security agencies therein. These phenomena have become quite common and don’t surprise anyone, especially as cybersecurity threats become more dangerous and sophisticated following the adoption of AI for hostile purposes. In May 2026, Presidential Decree No. 1258 vested the National Security Committee (KNB) of the Republic of Kazakhstan with additional responsibilities, including in the digital domain. Largely construed as routine modernization efforts, the KNB’s new responsibilities may not have attracted much scrutiny and may have therefore flown under public’s radar, as security agencies worldwide play an increasingly bigger role in cybersecurity. Buried in the bureaucratic language of Decree No. 1258 are three clauses that go well beyond routine oversight. Together, they don’t just make the KNB a “watchdog” over digitalization, but also give it the legal standing to become a direct participant in Kazakhstan’s AI buildout, with the authority to draw private industry into its orbit. Section 14 now enables the KNB to develop, purchase, and operate, among others, digital systems, armament, and equipment and – for these purposes – to sign contracts with state bodies and organizations of the Republic of Kazakhstan regardless of ownership form, with special services, and with organizations of foreign states. In Section 15, Clauses 224-2 and 224-3 vest the KNB with the responsibility to execute the state’s AI policy and the authority to develop and deploy artificial intelligence models and software products. On the surface, these clauses point at data and critical infrastructure protection efforts, and some may even be tempted to attribute these new responsibilities to a growing problem with data leaks in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina’s Remarks Spark Bangladesh’s Boldest Message to India Yet
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh’s latest diplomatic protest against India is significant not simply because of its unusually strong language, but because of what it reveals about how Dhaka wants its post-2024 political reality — and its relationship with New Delhi — to be understood. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs under the Tarique Rahman-led Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government issued the statement on Wednesday night after former prime minister Sheikh Hasina addressed supporters and the media from New Delhi on the second anniversary of the July movement that led to her ouster in August 2024. In her comments, Hasina rejected allegations surrounding the July-August crackdown, defended her government’s actions, criticized Bangladesh’s current leadership, called for the ban on the Awami League to be lifted, and said she planned to return to Bangladesh. Dhaka responded with one of its strongest diplomatic statements against India since the political transition two years ago. It accused New Delhi of allowing Hasina to use Indian soil to launch “venomous vitriol” against Bangladesh, despite prior concerns conveyed to the Indian government about the possible consequences for efforts to reset bilateral ties. The Foreign Ministry described Hasina as an “absconding convicted genocider,” a “convicted mass murderer,” and the head of a “mafia enterprise,” while calling her media appearance “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh” and “a grievous insult to the martyrs” of what it repeatedly referred to as the “July Revolution.” India, for its part, had earlier maintained that the program was organized by a private entity and that the government neither organized nor endorsed the event or the views expressed there. But beyond the diplomatic exchange, the statement itself merits closer attention. A careful reading suggests it marks an important evolution in Bangladesh’s official messaging toward India.

articles.title: US Pacific Command Considers Moving Billions in Planned Infrastructure Out of Micronesia
articles.excerpt: Negotiation failures are leading U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM) to look for alternative locations for the $2 billion Department of Defense investment in infrastructure in Yap, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). On June 29, 2026, Admiral Samuel Paparo, the PACOM commander, wrote to President Wesley Simina of FSM that the country’s demand for a “$1.3 billion compensation package is unreasonable, unanchored to demonstrable costs, and divergent from the spirit of our partnership under the Compact of Free Association.” As a result, “U.S. PACOM intends to move forward by assessing alternative locations across the region to meet the needs of Pacific defense.” Yap state, made up over a hundred islands, is a core part of the Second Island Chain. The main island in Yap state, also called Yap, is just over 500 miles southwest of Guam. The strategic importance of the Yap group of islands was proven toward the end of World War II. After the United States took the region from Japan, one of Yap’s atolls, Ulithi, became the largest and busiest American naval base in the world. Map by Cleo Paskal and Pavak Patel. FSM’s Compact of Free Association With the U.S. In the decades after the war, Yap joined with neighboring island groups to form the independent country of Federated States of Micronesia. FSM then signed a Compact of Free Association (COFA) with the United States that ties the two countries together in profound ways, including the citizens of FSM being allowed to live and work freely in the U.S. Additionally, according to COFA, the “Government of the United States has full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters in or relating to the Federated States of Micronesia.” This goes far beyond usual U.S.

articles.title: As Taiwan’s Drone Budget Debate Drags on, Time Is Running out
articles.excerpt: Taiwan’s government proposed a NT$1.25 trillion (US$40 billion) special defense budget in November 2025 – including its first large-scale procurement of more than 210,000 drones. That was finally passed in May 2026, but with a substantial change: the opposition-led legislature removed all funding for domestically produced drones. In June 2026, the Ministry of National Defense (MND) advanced a NT$210 billion procurement proposal, which led to the introduction of competing bills by each party. The legislature finally completed committee review for the budget on July 27, but there was no agreement. The parties could not reach consensus on any provision in their competing bills, leaving all bills intact for further negotiations. A floor vote could come as early as late August, but if the opposition majority’s version prevails, funding would not pass until early 2027 even under the most optimistic scenario. That means Taiwan could end 2026 without awarding a single new large-scale contract for domestically produced combat drones. This delay exposes the central danger of the prolonged budget review: Taiwan is falling further behind China’s procurement pace and losing ground as its partners accelerate their own acquisition of uncrewed systems. China has reportedly ordered nearly 1 million drones for delivery by 2026; Ukraine plans to produce 7 million this year; the U.S. Army aims to acquire at least 1 million over the next two to three years; and Japan has allocated 277 billion yen (US$1.7 billion) to rapidly expand its drone arsenal. Taiwan’s military, by contrast, holds less than 5,000 drones. A second tranche of 2,032 U.S.-supplied ALTIUS systems has received executive and congressional approval in Washington but remains under contract negotiation, with delivery to Taiwan’s inventory still pending. In an era of drone warfare driven by mass production, testing, and data-enabled software iteration, a one-year procurement gap could prove fatal for Taiwan.

articles.title: India at a Crossroads: Examining Comprehensive National Power and the Road to 2047
articles.excerpt: Turbulence and conflicts have dominated the first six years of the 2020s. Events like the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, and the conflict in West Asia have disrupted the normal way of life across the world. COVID-19 disrupted global supply chains, exposing the vulnerabilities of nations dependent on some others for critical needs. That forced nations to look inwards, focusing on self-sufficiency and self-reliance. The Russia-Ukraine war that followed soon after further exposed key vulnerabilities in global security as well as intertwined issues of trade dependency and connectivity. However, the mother of all disruptions has resulted from the war in Iran, leading to closure of sea traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical choke point through which almost 20 percent of world’s crude oil and other petroleum products transit. The conflict is thus causing an unprecedented global energy crisis. Yet India has been able to wade through these multiple crises successfully and its economy still continues to grow steadily. India developed a COVID-19 vaccine, which it exported to more than 110 countries. India thus won the trust and respect of the world. When the Russia-Ukraine war broke out, it was India’s message that resonated across the globe: “this is not the era of war.” Simultaneously, it withstood pressure from Europe and the United States and continued to buy crude oil from Russia to safeguard its energy security and exercise strategic autonomy. Amid the ongoing war in Iran, India was quick on its feet to secure supplies of crude oil. As a result, India has successfully diversified its import basket and met its crude oil import requirements of 5 million barrels per day in June and July. India is already the world’s fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP. It has one of the world’s largest armed forces, which proved their mettle during Operation Sindoor in May 2025.

articles.title: Malaysia Says It Will Not Deport Rohingya if There Are Risks to Their Safety
articles.excerpt: Malaysia’s government said yesterday that it will not proceed with the planned repatriation of 5,000 Myanmar refugees if their lives are found to be at risk upon their return. Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni announced recently that around 5,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the immigration detention depot are set to be repatriated as soon as Myanmar is ready to accept them – a fact that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed on July 30. “We have good ​relations with Myanmar. They have now agreed to take 5,000 Rohingya from Malaysia,” Anwar said during a campaign rally in Negeri Sembilan state. Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil told a press briefing yesterday that the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Home Affairs are currently reviewing the plan to identify the 5,000 refugees to be returned to Myanmar, “Malaysia, as ​a responsible country, will not return the 5,000 Myanmar refugees if they would ​either be persecuted or their lives would be threatened,” he said, as per Reuters, adding that there were “several matters” that needed to be discussed with the authorities in Myanmar. “The Prime ⁠Minister has taken note that we cannot send them back if their lives are threatened,” he said. “So there are several matters ​currently being studied by the Foreign Ministry.” The deportation plan follows a recent upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric and public hostility toward Rohingya Muslims, particularly online. In the past few months, prominent public figures have since described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country, while Rohingya refugee schools across the country ​have been forced to close due to harassment and ⁠threats. Late last month, more than 100 refugees were detained by the authorities after gathering outside the UNHCR building in Kuala Lumpur to ​seek assistance, after being evicted from their settlement in Penang state.

articles.title: Artillery-Missile Command: Vietnam’s Answer to the Maritime-Continental Dilemma
articles.excerpt: Vietnam’s military modernization is setting off in a new direction. Instead of procuring naval platforms such as submarines or frigates to defend its South China Sea claims, as it did in the 2010s, the country is looking to upgrade and acquire long-range surface-to-surface and ground-based anti-ship missiles (ASMs) to guard against both continental and maritime threats. A number of recent developments show that this is the case. First, Vietnam established the Artillery-Missile Command based on the Artillery Corps in August of last year. The Command was intended to be leaner, given expanded duties, and equipped with more advanced weaponry. Second, it introduced the domestically produced shore-based ASM system Truong Son and showed off the Scud-B tactical ballistic missiles procured from the Soviet Union in the 1980s, on the 80th anniversary of Vietnam’s founding. Hanoi also revealed that it succeeded in upgrading the range of the Scud-B from 300 to 500 kilometers. In May, Vietnam signed a $629 million BrahMos missile deal with India. Third, it is moving the 380th Missile Brigade from Thai Nguyen province in northern Vietnam to Dak Lak province in the Central Highlands, whose mountainous terrain and position at the center of the Indochinese peninsula can help Vietnam project power further southwest in response to security uncertainty from Cambodia. The 380th Missile Brigade is one of Vietnam’s two ballistic missile brigades, along with the 490th Missile Brigade based in Hai Phong in the northeast. Vietnam’s rationale for this focus on missile forces is rooted in the maritime-continental dilemma. As I argued a few years ago, Vietnam is torn between allocating its resources to the continental west and the maritime east. Land-based platforms such as tanks, artillery, or armored personnel carriers cannot be deployed to defend the country’s outposts in the South China Sea. Frigates, submarines, or patrol boats likewise cannot guard Vietnam’s borders with Laos and Cambodia.

C’est l’occasion pour nous de vous rediriger vers cet étonnant reportage-portrait : Lire aussi : Le 09/08 à 21:44 La Russie affirme avoir détruit 285 drones ukrainiens au cours de la journée de dimanche Le ‌ministère de la défense russe a déclaré, dimanche, que ses ​unités de ‌défense aérienne avaient intercepté et détruit 285 drones ukrainiens en l’espace d’une douzaine d’heures. Ces drones ont ⁠été ‌abattus entre 8 heures et 20 heures, ​heure de Moscou (7 heures à 19 heures à Paris), principalement dans ‌le ‌centre et de ⁠l’ouest de ‌la ‌Russie, mais aussi dans la ​région du Bachkortostan, entre ‌la Volga et l’Oural, selon le ministère. Le maire de Moscou, Sergueï Sobianine, a écrit sur Telegram que les unités de défense aérienne ​avaient détruit cinq drones qui se dirigeaient vers la capitale.

articles.title: Israel lehnt 15-Punkte-Friedensplan von Donald Trump für Gaza ab
articles.excerpt: Israel weist den Plan des Gaza-Friedensrats für eine Entwaffnung der islamistischen Terrororganisation Hamas und einen Abzug Israels aus dem Gazastreifen zurück. »Israel lehnt das 15-Punkte-Dokument ab«, sagte der israelische Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanyahu während einer Kabinettssitzung in Jerusalem. »Die israelische Armee wird keinerlei Abzug vollziehen, bis die Hamas entwaffnet ist«, sagte Netanyahu ferner. Dabei beziehe er sich ausdrücklich auf alle Waffen, nicht nur schwere. Außerdem bekräftigte der Regierungschef seine Ablehnung eines unabhängigen palästinensischen Staates. Der Friedensrat hatte allerdings vor knapp einer Woche bereits mitgeteilt, man erwarte von Israel erst nach einer Entwaffnung der Hamas einen kompletten Abzug aus dem Küstenstreifen.Nach dem Fahrplan des Friedensrats sollen Israel und die Hamas die Kämpfe einstellen. Eine palästinensische Übergangsverwaltung soll mit Unterstützung einer internationalen Stabilisierungstruppe die Kontrolle über Verwaltung und Sicherheit übernehmen. Zudem ist ein Abzug der israelischen Armee vorgesehen. Die von der Hamas unter internationaler Aufsicht übergebenen Waffen sollen anschließend unter palästinensischer Kontrolle bleiben. Dies lehnt Israel jedoch ab und fordert, die Waffen müssten aus dem Gazastreifen entfernt werden.

articles.title: Sommerinterview mit Luigi Pantisano von Die Linke: Vergesellschaftung als Allheilmitteln
articles.excerpt: Verstaatlichung als Allheilmitteln? Mit Palme im Nacken sinniert Luigi Pantisano im ZDF-Sommerinterview leicht verdöst, mit welcher Radikalkur er Deutschland sanieren will. Vielleicht sogar mit der CDU. Zumindest in Sachsen-Anhalt.

articles.title: Tupac Shakur: Mordprozess gegen mutmaßlichen Täter beginnt in Las Vegas
articles.excerpt: Fast 30 Jahre nach dem Mord von Rapper Tupac Shakur beginnt das Gerichtsverfahren gegen Duane »Keffe D« Davis, dem die Staatsanwaltschaft vorwirft, den Mord im Jahr 1996 organisiert zu haben. Er steht in Las Vegas im US-Bundesstaat Nevada vor Gericht. Davis ist unter anderem wegen Mordes mit Gebrauch einer tödlichen Waffe angeklagt. Er sitzt bereits seit 2023 im Gefängnis und hat auf nicht schuldig plädiert.Das Verfahren wird voraussichtlich etwa einen Monat dauern. Es gilt als unwahrscheinlich, dass dabei auch aufgeklärt wird, wer auf Shakur geschossen hat. Die Staatsanwaltschaft will jedoch beweisen, dass Davis der Drahtzieher des Mordes war und die Tatwaffe zur Verfügung stellte. Davis’ Anwälte sagten hingegen, es gebe keine Beweise, dass er den Mord angeordnet habe.Der Angeklagte selbst hatte in den vergangenen Jahren mehrfach öffentlich darüber gesprochen, dass er in dem weißen Cadillac gesessen habe, aus dem 1996 in Las Vegas die Schüsse auf Tupac Shakur abgefeuert wurden. Er sei der einzige Insasse aus dem Auto, der noch lebe, hatte der 63-Jährige in Interviews gesagt. Die tödlichen Schüsse habe aber sein Neffe abgegeben, so der Verdächtige. Der besagte Neffe war 1998 selbst bei einer Schießerei ums Leben gekommen. Der 25-jährige Shakur war in der Tatnacht am 7. September 1996 mit Suge Knight, Mitbegründer des für Gangsta-Rap bekannten Labels Death Row Records, unterwegs. Er starb sechs Tage nach der Tat im Krankenhaus.Shakur gehörte zu den erfolgreichsten Rap-Künstlern der Neunzigerjahre. Der Hip-Hop-Star war zeitweise in Drogenhandel und andere Kriminalität verwickelt, er kam auch ins Gefängnis. Millionen Fans weltweit verehren den Rapper und seine Musik noch immer.

articles.title: USA: Pentagon ruft Industrie auf, schneller Waffen zu produzieren
articles.excerpt: Das Pentagon hat Vertreter der US-Rüstungsindustrie dazu aufgefordert, die Produktion und Lieferung von Waffen rasch zu steigern. Das berichten die »Washington Post« und der US-Sender CNN übereinstimmend unter Berufung auf eine Mitteilung eines Ministeriumsvertreters. Pentagon-Sprecher Sean Parnell bestätigte der Deutschen Presse-Agentur die Echtheit des Dokuments. Es fällt in eine Zeit, in der Experten und Berichte von US-Medien zuletzt immer wieder auf schwindende Waffenreserven im US-Militär als Folge des Irankriegs hingewiesen hatten. US-Präsident Donald Trump wies das zurück.Der stellvertretende US-Verteidigungsminister Steve Feinberg habe Vertretern der Rüstungsindustrie am Mittwoch eine Frist von maximal drei Wochen übermittelt, um Pläne vorzulegen, die schnellere Liefertermine und/oder eine gesteigerte Produktion für kritische Fähigkeiten vorsähen, zitieren CNN und die »Washington Post« aus dem Dokument. Laut der Zeitung soll Feinberg darin eine klare Erwartung geäußert haben: »Jahrelange Entwicklungszyklen sind nicht akzeptabel.« Man müsse die Pläne drastisch beschleunigen und die Produktionskapazitäten jetzt ausbauen, zitiert ihn die »Washington Post« weiter. Was der Pentagon-Sprecher sagtSeit dem ersten Tag von Pete Hegseth als US-Verteidigungsminister konzentriere sich das Pentagon darauf, einen Wandel hinsichtlich der Geschwindigkeit, Kapazität und Schlagkraft der amerikanischen Verteidigungsindustrie herbeizuführen, betonte Parnell in einem Statement. Hegseths Stellvertreter Feinberg arbeite daran, ein veraltetes Beschaffungssystem zu reformieren. »Direkt mit führenden Vertretern der Industrie zusammenzuarbeiten, um die Produktion zu beschleunigen, ist nichts Neues.«

articles.excerpt: Die Schweizer Demokratie wird oft als vorbildlich bezeichnet. Doch als die Weltkriege das Land auf die Probe stellten, warf die Eidgenossenschaft demokratische Werte schnell über Bord. Auch heute gilt Teilhabe nicht für alle.

articles.title: Iran: Mohsen Resai übernimmt Vorsitz im Nationalen Sicherheitsrat
articles.excerpt: Der ehemalige Kommandeur der iranischen Revolutionswächter, Mohsen Resai, ist neuer Vorsitzender des iranischen Nationalen Sicherheitsrates. Der oberste Führer Mojtaba Khamenei habe ihn ernannt, teilten iranische Medien übereinstimmend mit. Khamenei schrieb dies auch selbst auf X . Mit Beginn des Irankriegs Ende Februar waren durch amerikanisch-israelische Luftangriffe viele zentrale Personen der iranischen Führung getötet worden. Dass nun der bisherige Vorsitzende des Sicherheitsrates, der eher unbekannte Brigadegeneral Mohammed Bagher-Zolghadr, durch Resai ersetzt wird, könnte auf eine weitere Festigung des Einflusses der Revolutionswächter auf die Regierung hindeuten.Erst am Vortag hatte Bagher-Zolghadr den USA eine ganze Liste an Bedingungen für ein Ende der Blockade der Straße von Hormus vorgelegt. Die Vereinigten Staaten dürften die Islamische Republik nie wieder bedrohen, hieß es in der von iranischen Staatsmedien veröffentlichten Erklärung des Nationalen Sicherheitsrates. Zudem müssten sie den Krieg gegen Iran und dessen Verbündete in der Region endgültig beenden. Generalmajor Resai gilt als eine der dienstältesten Figuren des iranischen Machtapparats: Bereits zu Zeiten des Schahs war er Teil einer Organisation, die mitunter gewaltsam den Boden für die islamische Revolution 1979 bereitete. Als 27-Jähriger wurde er während des Iran-Irak-Kriegs Kommandeur der iranischen Revolutionswächter. In den vergangenen Jahren widmete er sich der Politik. Er gilt als einflussreiche Figur in Sicherheitskreisen. Die argentinische Staatsanwaltschaft benannte Resai als einen der Hinterleute eines schweren Bombenanschlags auf eine jüdische Gemeinde in Buenos Aires 1994. Der Nationale Sicherheitsrat gilt als ein zentrales Kontrollgremium innerhalb der Islamischen Republik. Das mächtige Gremium befasst sich mit Fragen rund um die nationale Sicherheit. Neben dem Präsidenten als Vorsitzenden gehören dem Rat mit rund einem Dutzend Mitgliedern mehrere Minister und Generäle an.

articles.title: »Die Odyssee« von Christopher Nolan: Die wichtigsten Fragen und Antworten
articles.excerpt: Lange gab es nicht mehr so viele leidenschaftliche Debatten über den Inhalt eines Kinofilms. Taugt Matt Damon als Odysseus? Ist es okay, den Namen mit US-amerikanischem Akzent auszusprechen? Sind die gezeigten Schiffe historisch akkurat? Hätten da nicht mehr Griechen mitspielen sollen? Und wo bleibt eigentlich die Erotik? Filmkritiker, Altphilologinnen und Elon Musk – alle haben eine starke Meinung zu Christopher Nolans Adaption der »Odyssee«. In gewisser Weise passt das zum Originalstoff. Denn auch an der Vorlage des Films, Homers Dichtung, arbeiteten sich bereits Generationen von Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftlern ab und fragten sich: Wie viel Realität steckt hinter der Geschichte von Odysseus? Und wie sollte sie interpretiert werden? Was ist die Odyssee? Und wer war Homer noch mal?Auch die »Odyssee«, 24 Gesänge mit mehr als 12.000 Versen, ist Fiktion. Zwar werden darin reale Orte und Akteure benannt, aber sie erzählt auch von Fabelwesen und Göttern. Die »Ilias«, das Vorgängerwerk, entstand um 700 vor Christus und erzählt von der Sage des Trojanischen Kriegs. Vermutlich einige Jahre später beschreibt die Odyssee die anschließende Heimreise des Helden Odysseus. Odysseus ist ein Held des trojanischen Krieges. Er ist es, der die Idee zur List des trojanischen Pferds hat. Nach zehn Jahren zermürbender Belagerung Trojas versteckt er sich mit einer Gruppe Soldaten im Bauch eines Holzpferdes, getarnt als Geschenk und Gottesopfer. Nachts öffneten die versteckten Griechen das Tor und eroberten die Stadt.Die Odyssee erzählt nun die Heimreise des Kriegshelden vorbei an verschiedenen Stationen, etwa der Zauberin Circe, den Sirenen oder dem Zyklopen Polyphem. Auf seiner Heimatinsel Ithaka wird seine Frau Penelope unterdessen von Freiern bedrängt. Als er nach zehn Jahren schließlich zurückkehrt, muss er um sie und sein Königreich kämpfen.Die Geschichte der Ilias, Gesang für Gesang nacherzählt, finden Sie hier .

articles.excerpt: Italiens Strände gehören zu den schönsten der Welt und sind ein dickes Geschäft. An vielen haben selbst Italiener nur Zutritt, wenn sie zahlen. Ein junger Politiker macht mit Instagram-Videos dagegen mobil.

articles.title: Nepal: Leichen von deutschem Bergsteiger und vier Vermissten geborgen
articles.excerpt: In Nepal sind die Leichen eines deutschen Bergsteigers und vier weiterer Vermisster geborgen worden. »Alle fünf Leichen wurden heute Morgen von einem Hubschrauber und unserem Rettungsteam geborgen«, sagte der Leiter des Expeditionsunternehmens Dreamers Destination, Phurba Tenjing Sherpa, am Sonntag der Nachrichtenagentur AFP. Die Bergung gelang neun Monate nach dem Lawinenunglück, bei dem die Bergsteiger uns Leben kamen. Die fünf Toten, neben dem Deutschen zwei Italiener und jeweils ein Kletterer aus Frankreich und Kanada, waren am Samstag entdeckt worden.Die Bergsteiger waren im November 2025 an den unteren Hängen des 5.630 Meter hohen Bergs Yalung Ri nahe der Grenze zu Tibet von einer Lawine erfasst worden. Nach dem Unglück suchten Rettungsmannschaften zunächst vergeblich nach den Vermissten. Die Leichen seien unter einer dicken Schneeschicht begraben gewesen, sagte Sherpa. Eine neue Suchaktion sei nun erfolgreich gewesen, »weil der Schnee diesmal geschmolzen war«. Die Bergung hatte sich zunächst wegen schlechten Wetters verzögert. Sobald sich das Wetter bessert, sollen die Toten nach Kathmandu geflogen werden, wie der Polizeivertreter Manoj Kumar Lama sagte.In Nepal befinden sich acht der zehn höchsten Berge der Welt, darunter der Mount Everest. Die Gipfel des Himalaja ziehen jedes Jahr tausende Bergsteiger und Wanderer an. Nach Angaben des Expeditionsarchivs Himalayan Database kamen seit 1950 mehr als tausend Menschen auf den Gipfeln des Landes ums Leben. Fast ein Drittel der Todesfälle wurde durch Lawinen verursacht.

articles.title: Ukraine-Krieg: Wie sich Tschernobyl gegen Russlands nächsten Invasionsversuch wappnet
articles.excerpt: Zu Beginn der Invasion besetzten Putins Truppen die Atomruine nördlich von Kyjiw. Heute herrscht die ukrainische Armee über das geisterhafte Gebiet. Und bereitet sich darauf vor, dass der Feind zurückkommt.

articles.title: Syrien: Damaskus und Moskau einigen sich auf Nutzung russischer Stützpunkte
articles.excerpt: Die syrische Übergangsregierung hat sich nach eigenen Angaben mit Russland darüber geeinigt, wie die beiden verbliebenen russischen Militärstützpunkte künftig genutzt werden sollen. Der Marinestützpunkt Tartus und der Luftwaffenstützpunkt Hmeimim sollten in »gemeinsame Ausbildungszentren« umgewandelt werden, meldete die syrische Nachrichtenagentur Sana unter Berufung auf das Außenministerium in Damaskus. Der Schritt erfolge im Rahmen neuer Vereinbarungen, welche »die beiderseitigen Interessen wahren« sollen, meldete die Agentur weiter. Die Umwandlung solle binnen drei Monaten vollzogen werden. Der Vereinbarung gingen anderthalb Jahre lang andauernde Verhandlungen voraus.Der Luftwaffenstützpunkt Hmeimim und der Marinestützpunkt Tartus sind die einzigen russischen Militärbasen im Ausland, die nicht in ehemaligen Sowjetstaaten liegen. Beide befinden sich im Westen Syriens an der Mittelmeerküste. Russland war ein wichtiger Verbündeter des syrischen Machthabers Baschar al-Assad während des 14 Jahre lang andauernden Bürgerkriegs in Syrien. Moskau unterstützte damals die syrische Armee, indem russische Soldaten Luftangriffe auf die von Dschihadisten kontrollierten Gebiete flogen.Nach Assads Sturz durch Dschihadisten im Dezember 2024 verlor Russland stark an Einfluss in der Region. Bei einem Besuch des syrischen Übergangspräsidenten Ahmed al-Sharaa in Moskau Ende Januar lobte der russische Präsident Wladimir Putin dessen Erfolge. Keiner der beiden sprach dabei die militärische Präsenz Russlands in Syrien an.

articles.title: Tour de France Femmes: Demi Vollering gewinnt erneut – Niedermaier bestes Nachwuchstalent
articles.excerpt: Damit revanchierte sich Vollering für die knappe Niederlage gegen Niewiadoma bei der Tour 2024, als die Polin im Radsportmekka Alpe d’Huez mit vier Sekunden Vorsprung vor der Niederländerin den Gesamtsieg feierte. Die neunte Etappe auf dem Rundkurs über 99,2 Kilometer mit vier Überquerungen des Col d’Èze wurde wieder zum Zweikampf der beiden Spitzenfahrerinnen. Beide setzten sich am letzten Anstieg ab, 500 Meter vor der letzten Bergwertung attackierte schließlich Vollering und holte sich den Sieg im Alleingang vor der Spanierin Paula Blasi. Die deutschen Fahrerinnen spielten bei der Entscheidung keine Rolle und warten damit seit 2023 weiter auf einen Etappensieg beim wichtigsten Frauenrennen.

articles.title: Schleswig-Holstein: Pilot stirbt bei Absturz von Kleinflugzeug
articles.excerpt: In Schleswig-Holstein ist beim Absturz eines Kleinflugzeugs ein Mensch ums Leben gekommen. Der Pilot der Maschine, der bei dem Unglück starb, war der einzige Insasse, wie die Feuerwehr mitteilte. Das Flugzeug sei am Mittag direkt neben dem Sportflugplatz Uetersen-Heist westlich von Hamburg in ein Feld gestürzt, teilte die Polizei mit. Einsatzkräfte von Polizei und Feuerwehr sind demnach an der Absturzstelle. Mitarbeiter der Braunschweiger Bundesstelle für Flugunfalluntersuchung seien ebenfalls auf dem Weg dorthin. Das Alter und Geschlecht des Toten waren zunächst nicht bekannt, ebenso die Ursache für den Absturz.

articles.title: Berlin: Hunderte Lehrer fallen wegen Krankheit dauerhaft aus
articles.excerpt: Fast 400 Lehrkräfte in Berlin fallen krankheitsbedingt seit mindestens einem Jahr aus. Das geht aus einer Antwort des Senats auf eine parlamentarische Anfrage des Abgeordneten Alexander King (BSW) hervor, die der Deutschen Presse-Agentur vorliegt und über die zuvor die »Berliner Morgenpost« berichtet hat. Den Angaben zufolge sind 225 verbeamtete Lehrer seit mindestens einem Jahr krankgeschrieben. Hinzu kommen 155 angestellte Lehrkräfte, die ebenfalls seit mindestens zwölf Monaten ausfallen. Insgesamt gibt es in der Hauptstadt etwa 35.000 Lehrerinnen und Lehrer.Der Abgeordnete King führt die Entwicklung auch auf die »mangelhafte Personalausstattung« zurück. Sie erhöhe die Belastung der vorhandenen Lehrkräfte und begünstige weitere krankheitsbedingte Ausfälle, erklärte King. Blickt man auf die Bezirke, gibt es die meisten langfristig kranken Lehrkräfte in Marzahn-Hellersdorf. Dahinter folgen Pankow und Lichtenberg. Am wenigsten Lehrkräfte fallen in Mitte sowie in Spandau und Tempelhof-Schöneberg aus.Bei Langzeiterkrankten wird laut Bildungsverwaltung die Zentrale Medizinische Gutachtenstelle (ZMGA) des Landesamts für Gesundheit und Soziales damit beauftragt, eine Untersuchung durchzuführen. »Besteht laut Gutachten der ZMGA keine Aussicht, dass die Beamtin oder der Beamte innerhalb weiterer sechs Monate wieder dienstfähig wird, beginnt die Einleitung des Ruhestandsverfahrens«, hieß es. Kann die betroffene Person nicht mehr als Lehrkraft arbeiten, ist aber in der Lage, andere Tätigkeiten zu übernehmen, kann »ein Einsatz im Projekt der beruflichen Neuorientierung durch amtsangemessene anderweitige Verwendung erfolgen«. An diesem Projekt nehmen derzeit 29 der Betroffenen teil, wie es hieß.21,6 Milliarden Euro kostet das Krankengeld die Kassen – weshalb nun bei den Langzeitpatienten gespart werden soll. Wie diese Gruppe jetzt schon drangsaliert und wie sehr das Problem vergrößert wird, lesen Sie hier .
